chapters.title: Chapter 6: Portfolio and Capital Allocation Across Regimes

lessons.title: Regime-Aware Position Sizing: Beyond Fixed Fractional Bets

body.text: Fixed-fractional betting assumes the same edge and the same risk every single day. Chapter 5 asked what mix of strategies deserves weight. This chapter asks the same question about how much capital, and the honest answer depends on which regime is actually live.

children.text: Chapter 5's compatibility matrix answers what to trade in a given regime. It says nothing about how much capital to put behind it. This lesson starts with the standard baseline for that question, fixed-fractional sizing, shows its more principled cousin, the Kelly criterion, and then does to Kelly exactly what this course has done to every fixed-parameter method so far: lets its inputs vary by regime.
The most common risk management convention in trading is fixed-fractional sizing: risk a constant percentage of account capital, commonly 1% or 2%, on every trade, regardless of market conditions.

body.caption: Fixed-fractional sizing: the same risk percentage, applied every day

children.text: The Kelly Criterion: A More Principled Version, With the Same Flaw
John Kelly's 1956 result gives the bet size that maximizes long-run geometric growth. For a continuous return series, it simplifies to a clean ratio of expected return to variance.

body.caption: Kelly fraction: expected return divided by return variance

children.text: Kelly is a genuine improvement over an arbitrary fixed percentage, it is derived, not guessed. But it shares the exact flaw this course keeps finding in fixed-parameter methods: mu and sigma-squared are treated as constants, one number each, for the entire time the strategy runs. That is the same assumption behind a single GARCH(1,1) fit in Chapter 4, and it fails for the same reason.
Regime-Aware Kelly: Reusing Chapter 3's Fitted Parameters

Chapter 3's HMM already estimated a mean and variance per regime. Plugging those directly into the Kelly formula, instead of one blended average across all regimes, gives a genuinely regime-aware bet size. Reuse Chapter 3 Lesson 1's illustrative calm and stressed parameters directly.

body.caption: Full Kelly fraction, computed per regime from Chapter 3's fitted parameters

body.text: Do not read +10.67x as an instruction. Raw Kelly applied to small daily equity edges routinely produces leverage figures far beyond what any sane risk desk would run, because a small mean divided by an even smaller variance can produce a very large ratio. This is precisely why almost nobody trades full Kelly in practice.

children.text: The standard practical fix is fractional Kelly, running some fraction of the full formula, commonly one-quarter or one-half, to absorb both the leverage problem above and a second, more fundamental issue: mu and sigma-squared are themselves estimates, not known truths, and Kelly is notoriously sensitive to errors in estimating them. A confident-looking edge that is actually noise can produce a full-Kelly bet size that is disastrously oversized. Fractional Kelly trims the position specifically to absorb that estimation risk.

body.caption: One-quarter Kelly, a common practical compromise

body.text: Notice what regime-aware Kelly does that fixed-fractional sizing structurally cannot: it does not just scale a single number up or down, it can flip sign entirely, from meaningfully long in the calm regime to meaningfully short in the stressed regime, because the fitted mean itself changes sign across regimes. A fixed-fractional rule, applied blindly, has no mechanism to do that at all; it only ever answers how much, never which direction the edge points.

children.text: Why This Still Isn't the Full Answer

This lesson's sizing quietly assumes you know the current regime with certainty. In practice you have a probability, not a certainty, exactly the filtered probabilities from Chapter 4's statsmodels output. The next lesson folds that uncertainty back in, alongside a second problem regime-aware Kelly does not address at all: what happens when several strategies, each with their own regime-aware sizing, all want to scale up their exposure to the same shared pool of capital at once.

body.title: Computing Kelly for a Third Regime
body.prompt: Using Chapter 3 Lesson 2's Elevated state parameters, mean -0.02% and standard deviation 1.30%, compute the full Kelly fraction f* = mu / sigma-squared. Express mu and sigma as decimals (e.g. 1.30% = 0.0130).
body.explanation: mu = -0.0002, sigma-squared = 0.0130² = 0.000169. f* = -0.0002 / 0.000169 ≈ -1.18. This sits between the Calm state's strongly positive Kelly fraction and the Stressed state's more negative one, exactly where an intermediate regime's fraction should fall.

body.title: Why Fractional Kelly, Not Full Kelly
body.question: Why do practitioners almost universally run a fraction of the Kelly formula, such as one-quarter or one-half Kelly, rather than the full formula?
options: Full Kelly is mathematically incorrect and needs to be corrected
Fractional Kelly compensates for the fact that mu and sigma-squared are estimates with real error, and tempers the often extreme leverage full Kelly implies for small daily edges
Fractional Kelly is required by SEBI regulation for all systematic strategies
Full Kelly only works for options strategies, not equities
body.explanation: Kelly's derivation assumes the inputs are known exactly. In practice they are estimated with error, and Kelly's growth-optimal formula is unforgiving of overestimating the edge, an error that a full-sized bet turns directly into oversized risk. Fractional Kelly is a deliberate, well-established buffer against exactly that estimation risk, not a sign the underlying math is wrong.

points: Fixed-fractional sizing risks a constant percentage of capital regardless of regime; the Kelly criterion improves on this by deriving position size from expected return and variance, f* = mu / sigma-squared
Kelly shares the same fixed-parameter flaw as a single GARCH fit: it assumes one mu and one sigma-squared hold for the whole sample, unless those inputs are made regime-specific

Plugging Chapter 3's fitted per-regime mean and variance into Kelly directly produces genuinely regime-aware sizing, including the ability to flip from long to short as the fitted mean changes sign across regimes
Full Kelly applied to small daily equity edges routinely implies extreme leverage, which is why fractional Kelly, commonly one-quarter or one-half, is the practical standard
Regime-aware Kelly still assumes certainty about the current regime; the next lesson folds in genuine regime uncertainty and the problem of multiple strategies competing for the same capital
